observations.text: SP, on the first exposure to arcing, maintained the DME arc only while the IP directed the timing of each correction turn and set up the initial roll-out on the assigned range. Radial-to-radial progress was tracked, but the SP did not independently establish the bearing pointer on the wingtip reference, so the range error reached 2.5 NM before the IP called the correction. Performance is at the desired MIF for this section but marginal; independent control of the arc radius is expected to develop over the following sorties.

SP, with the bearing pointer set close to the wingtip reference, flew the arc using 10 to 20 degree correction turns and required only the IP's verbal prompts to initiate them. Deviations reached the +/- 2 NM DME limit and were recognized and corrected after the prompt, without any IP control input. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP kept the bearing pointer within 10 degrees of the wingtip reference and adjusted the arc radius with small heading changes as the DME began to drift. Deviations did not exceed 1.5 NM DME and were recognized and corrected in a timely manner, without IP prompting or intervention. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP established the arc with a correct lead point at the assigned range and thereafter held the bearing pointer on the wingtip reference through each correction turn. DME was maintained within 0.6 NM of the assigned arc, with wind correction applied on the drift-affected quadrant. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP flew the arc on VOR-TACAN with GPS in OBS mode as an independent cross-check, anticipating each correction turn before the DME started to move. Deviations from the assigned arc remained negligible, within 0.2 NM, and the Basic A/C Control criteria were met throughout with accurate altitude and airspeed control. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to an incorrect wingtip reference technique that placed the bearing pointer well ahead of the 90 degree position, allowed the aircraft to fly through the assigned arc instead of turning to regain it. The arc was not maintained within the +/- 2 NM DME limit, the DME reaching 2.7 NM outside the assigned range, and the IP had to direct the intercept heading and fly part of the correction.

SP, due to mode confusion over the selected avionics mode and what it was protecting, followed GPS OBS course guidance while the range information still came from the TACAN, and did not maintain the assigned arc. The incorrect selection was not identified before the aircraft state changed, with the result that the range error exceeded the +/- 2 NM DME limit and reached 3 NM, and the IP directed the return to the arc. Positive identification of the active navigation source is required before the next instrument sortie.

SP maintained the arc within the desired standards for this section, holding the DME at the +/- 2 NM limit on two occasions on the upwind portion of the arc. The correction turns were initiated after the IP's verbal prompts, so the deviations were recognized and corrected with delay. Performance is marginal for the Training Section; earlier detection of the DME trend is expected to improve.

SP applied 10 to 20 degree correction turns and kept the bearing pointer close to the wingtip reference for the full arc. Deviations were limited to 1.5 NM DME and were recognized and corrected in a timely manner, without IP intervention. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP established the arc at the correct lead point and maintained it with accurate small heading corrections, applying wind correction on the drift-affected quadrant. DME was held within 0.5 NM of the assigned arc and the Basic A/C Control criteria were met throughout. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP flew the arc on VOR-TACAN and cross-checked it against GPS in OBS mode, anticipating each correction before the DME trend developed. Deviations from the assigned arc remained negligible at 0.2 NM, with altitude and airspeed held without any degradation of the instrument cross-check. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to correction turns of excessive magnitude applied late in the arc, over-controlled the aircraft across the assigned range instead of holding the bearing pointer at the wingtip reference. The arc was not maintained within the +/- 2 NM DME limit, with excursions of 2.6 NM inside and 2.4 NM outside the assigned range, and the IP had to fly part of the arc to re-establish the aircraft. Review of the arcing technique is required before the next sortie.

SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check while attention remained on the navigation display, did not monitor the DME readout during the correction turns and did not maintain the assigned arc. The result was a range error beyond the +/- 2 NM DME limit, reaching 2.8 NM, combined with a 300 ft altitude loss, and the IP directed and executed part of the correction.

SP, due to a late lead point at arc interception, rolled out beyond the assigned range and then used heading corrections too small to regain it. The DME reached the +/- 2 NM limit and the arc was regained only after the IP's verbal prompts, with recognition and correction occurring with delay.

SP, due to poor workload distribution, with navigation, communication and aircraft control attempted simultaneously, did not reassess the DME while transmitting the position report. The deviation from the assigned arc grew to the +/- 2 NM limit and was corrected only after the IP prompted a check of the DME readout. The error was recognized and corrected with delay, without IP control input.

SP maintained the assigned arc within the desired standards, with the DME twice drifting to 1.8 NM on the downwind quadrant before the correction turn was initiated. Both deviations were recognized and corrected without IP intervention. Performance is at the desired MIF for this section but marginal; tighter control of the arc radius through earlier wind correction is expected to improve.

SP established the arc using the correct lead point and maintained the bearing pointer on the wingtip reference with 10 degree correction turns. DME was held within 0.7 NM of the assigned arc throughout, with accurate and timely control inputs and no IP prompting. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP flew the arc on VOR-TACAN with GPS in OBS mode cross-checked, anticipating the wind effect on each quadrant of the arc before the DME began to move. Deviations remained negligible at 0.2 NM DME and the Basic A/C Control criteria were exceeded, with altitude and heading control unaffected by the navigation task. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to reference to the course deviation indicator rather than the DME readout as the primary control parameter for the arc, applied corrections that did not address the range error. The assigned arc was not maintained within the +/- 2 NM DME limit, the aircraft reaching 3 NM outside the assigned range, and the IP directed the intercept and flew part of the correction.

SP, due to over-reliance on automation that was not fully understood, followed the GPS OBS course line without an independent check of the DME against the assigned arc. The result was a range error beyond the +/- 2 NM DME limit, reaching 2.9 NM, which was not detected until the IP intervened and took control to re-establish the arc. Independent raw-data monitoring of the arc radius is required.

SP, due to correction turns initiated only after the DME had already moved rather than at the wingtip reference cue, allowed the arc radius to decay progressively through the turn. The DME reached the +/- 2 NM limit and the arc was regained only after the IP's verbal prompts, with the deviation recognized and corrected with delay.

SP, due to distraction from the primary scan by an unrelated switch action, stopped monitoring the DME during the second half of the arc. The deviation reached the +/- 2 NM limit before the IP's verbal prompt, after which the SP re-established the assigned range without IP control input. The error was recognized and corrected with delay.

SP, due to late application of wind correction on the downwind quadrant, allowed the aircraft to drift outside the assigned range before initiating the correction turn. The DME reached 1.6 NM, a minor deviation that was recognized and corrected in a timely manner, without IP intervention.

SP, due to an error that went undetected because the cross-check was not re-established after the navigation aid was retuned, did not verify the DME source against the arc facility for a short period. The range error grew to 1.5 NM before the SP identified it and corrected it without IP intervention, with altitude and airspeed maintained throughout.

SP maintained the assigned arc within the +/- 1 NM DME standard, with the DME reaching 0.9 NM on two occasions before the correction turn was initiated. The corrections were accurate and applied without IP prompting, but the arc was held toward the outer edge of the desired band rather than on the assigned range. Performance is at the desired MIF but marginal for this section; earlier anticipation of the correction turn is expected to improve consistency.

SP flew the arc on VOR-TACAN with GPS in OBS mode as a cross-check, anticipating each correction turn from the bearing pointer position before the DME began to move. Deviations from the assigned arc remained negligible, within 0.2 NM, with altitude, airspeed and heading control unaffected by the navigation workload. Above end of block MIF achieved.
